an0037.user: Eyewear brand, running Meesho ads. I think there's a leak somewhere in my funnel but I'm fairly new and not sure where to even look. What's the non-obvious thing I'm probably missing?
an0037.assistant:
The non-obvious thing is that 'a leak somewhere' isn't one problem — it's three possible problems at three different stages, and you can't fix it until you know which stage drops. So don't guess; measure. Pull your last 30 days as four counts:

- Visits → add-to-cart: if few people add, your product page or your traffic quality is the leak.
- Add-to-cart → checkout: a drop here is almost always shipping cost or a price surprise shown too late.
- Checkout → purchase: a drop here is payment friction — forced login, no UPI, no COD, a mobile checkout that fails.

Whichever transition has the steepest fall is your leak. That's the whole diagnosis. Get me those four numbers and I'll point at the exact step — and for eyewear on Meesho, my money's on the last two, but I won't pretend to know until I see it.

an0038.user: B2B SaaS for CA firms, Google Search. Last 30 days: 680K impressions, 8,159 clicks, CTR 1.2%, but only 96 orders — conversion rate 1.18%. AOV ₹2,150, running broad-match keywords. My CTR is the problem, right? People aren't clicking enough. I want to improve the ad copy to lift CTR.
an0038.assistant:
Your CTR isn't the problem, and lifting it would make things worse, not better. Look at where the funnel actually breaks.

8,159 clicks producing 96 orders is a 1.18% conversion rate. That's the rotten number. You're getting plenty of clicks — the issue is who's clicking. Broad-match keywords are spraying your ad across loosely related searches, so you're paying for 8,000 browsers, students, and curious accountants who were never going to buy your software. More clicks from the same broad-match net just means more of the wrong people.

That's intent mismatch, not a copy problem. CTR measures whether your ad is interesting; conversion measures whether the person had buying intent. Yours says: interesting enough, but aimed at the wrong crowd.

The fix runs the opposite direction from what you proposed. Stop optimising for clicks. Pull out of broad-match into phrase or exact match on high-intent terms — the searches where someone is actively shopping for CA-firm software, not just reading about it. Add a negative keyword list to block the junk queries eating your budget. Your CTR may even drop, and that's fine — you'll be paying for fewer, better clicks that actually convert. Chase qualified traffic, not clicks.

an0039.user: Pet-care brand, running a Meta + Google mix. Narrow question — why is my CTR low? Last 30 days: AOV ₹1,100, margin 58%, CAC ₹252, ROAS 4.4, repeat 7%, CTR 2.5%.
an0039.assistant:
Your CTR is 2.5% — that's not low, that's good. You're staring at the one healthy number while the actual problem sits right next to it, unread.

Here's the real picture. First-order contribution = ₹1,100 × 58% − ₹252 = ₹638 − ₹252 = +₹386. Acquisition is genuinely strong: cheap CAC, 4.4 ROAS, solid margin. The machine that brings you a first-time buyer works beautifully. So forget CTR; nothing's wrong there.

What's broken is what happens after. 90-day repeat is 7%. In pet-care — food, treats, supplements, the most reorder-driven category there is — 93 of every 100 buyers never come back. That's not a small inefficiency, it's the whole long game leaking out the bottom. You're profitable on order one and then the customer vanishes, so your lifetime value barely exceeds that single ₹386.

And this is exactly the trap: those great acquisition numbers will tempt you to scale spend. Don't, not yet — you'd just be buying more first orders into a bucket with no bottom, faster. Fix repeat first. Why does a pet owner not reorder food they presumably keep needing? Set up a reorder reminder around their run-out date, a subscribe-and-save, a 30-day follow-up. Move that 7% and the same ad spend suddenly compounds. The CTR was never the question.

an0040.user: Dental clinic, Google Search ads. I've stalled — new patient numbers won't grow. I'm sure it's my budget, I just need to spend more, right? That's the bottleneck.
an0040.assistant:
Maybe — but 'just spend more' is the most expensive wrong answer in marketing, and for a clinic it usually is wrong, because your bottleneck is more often the room than the budget. Before you raise spend, get me three numbers:

- Cost per booked appointment now, and how it's moved as you've spent more. If it's climbing, you've saturated your local search demand — more budget buys pricier, worse clicks, not more patients. Spending more makes that worse.
- Lead-to-booking rate. If enquiries come in but don't become appointments, the leak is your front desk or follow-up, and no ad budget fixes that.
- What a patient is worth over a year, not one visit — so we can even tell whether spending more would be profitable if it did work.

A dental clinic serves a small geographic catchment; Google Search there has a hard ceiling on how many people are actively searching for a dentist nearby. You may have already found it. Pull those three and we'll know if the bottleneck is budget, booking, or a maxed-out local market. Don't pour money into a ceiling.

an0041.user: Apparel label on Amazon. I've had this feeling my sales have softened — like the trend's turned against me and I should brace for it. Hard to say exactly, it's more a pattern I sense across the last while. Should I be worried?

Line those weeks up and the 'pattern' usually resolves into either a clear slope or random scatter. Bring them back and I'll tell you which. Don't brace for a downturn you might be imagining.

an0042.user: Footwear brand, Meesho ads, and I want the sharp read. Over six weeks my CAC has climbed from ₹391 to ₹799 and ROAS halved from 6.1 to 3.0. AOV ₹2,400, margin 62%. Frequency's at 3.8. I haven't changed creatives or audience — it's the exact setup that was printing money six weeks ago. Algorithm gone bad, or am I missing something?
an0042.assistant:
You're missing the simplest explanation, and it's hiding in the one number you mentioned almost in passing: frequency 3.8.

That's the smoking gun. Frequency above ~2.5 means the same people are seeing the same ad over and over; at 3.8 your audience has watched your creative nearly four times and made up their minds. The ones who'd buy have bought; the rest are now just scrolling past — which is exactly why CTR is sliding and CAC has doubled. You're paying rising prices to re-show a worn-out ad to people who are sick of it. That's textbook creative fatigue.

It is not the algorithm and not your targeting. Both are unchanged and faithful — that's the whole point. When inputs hold constant and output decays, the thing that moved is the audience's patience, and frequency 3.8 proves it.

The damage so far is contained: contribution is still ₹2,400 × 62% − ₹799 = +₹689, so you're profitable. But the slope is the warning — left alone, fatigue keeps pushing CAC up until that cushion's gone.

The move is fresh creative — genuinely new angles, not a recolour of the winner — and a testing cadence so the next challenger is always loading before the current ad tires. Riding one winning creative until it dies is why founders keep landing back here. Build the conveyor, not the single hero.

an0043.assistant:
Not paranoid — leaning your whole business on one channel is a genuine fragility, the kind that feels fine right up until a CPM spike or a policy change halves your sales overnight. But whether you're at 'sensible concentration' or 'one bad week from a crisis' depends on numbers I don't have. Pull these:

- The actual revenue split by channel. 'Almost everything' could be 65% or 92% from YouTube — those are very different risk levels, and the fix scales with the number.
- 90-day repeat rate. A strong repeat base is a shock absorber: even if YouTube wobbles, returning customers keep buying. Thin repeat means every channel hiccup hits revenue instantly.
- Your contribution per order on YouTube. If the golden channel is also your only profitable one, the dependence is doubly dangerous.

Get me those and we'll size the real exposure. If it's as concentrated as your gut suspects, the move is to deliberately stand up a second channel while YouTube is still strong — you build the lifeboat in calm water, not during the storm. But let's confirm the number first.

an0044.user: Pet-care brand on Amazon. I keep pouring effort into the marketing — better ads, better targeting — but profitability won't budge. I want your read: is my marketing underperforming, or is something else going on?
an0044.assistant:
The fact that better ads and better targeting haven't moved profit is itself the clue — when marketing improvements don't reach the bottom line, the problem usually isn't marketing at all, it's margin. But I won't declare that without seeing your economics. Three numbers:

- AOV and gross margin after Amazon's cut. Marketplace fees, FBA, storage, returns — these quietly eat pet-care margins, and if your real post-fee margin is thin, no amount of ad tuning can squeeze profit out of it.
- Your CAC. Put it against contribution (AOV × margin − CAC) and we'll see whether you're even profitable per order, or running a beautifully optimised loss.
- 90-day repeat. Pet-care should reorder; if it doesn't, you're buying every sale fresh, which crushes profit no matter how sharp the targeting.

Pull those and the picture will be obvious. My strong suspicion: you've been optimising the marketing because that's the knob you can see, while the real constraint is a margin too thin to leave anything behind. Numbers will tell us — get them and we'll know exactly which knob actually matters.

an0045.user: Gym, selling memberships and merch through Amazon Ads. Here's the dump, tell me what's wrong: ₹11L spend last 30 days, AOV ₹2,550, gross margin 69%, CAC ₹1,370, ROAS 1.9, CTR 1.4%, 90-day repeat 38%. That ROAS under 2 is killing me.

So your real per-customer contribution is well north of ₹390 — the first sale clears ₹390, and every repeat after that is almost pure margin on a 69%-margin product. That's a strong account.

You've been judging a healthy, high-margin, high-repeat business by the one metric built to scare you. The ₹390 first-order cushion is solid and the repeat behind it is real, so this account's signal is clear: scale it. Push spend up while watching CAC against your ₹1,759 breakeven — you've got a wide runway before order-one even gets tight. Stop staring at ROAS 1.9; it's been lying to you about a winner.

an0046.user: Vertical SaaS for clinics, acquiring through Google Performance Max. Last 30 days: AOV ₹1,650, margin 50%, CAC ₹374, ROAS 4.4, 90-day repeat 7%, CTR 2.4%. My CAC is the issue, isn't it — I need to get acquisition cheaper.
an0046.assistant:
Your CAC is the one thing you don't need to touch. At ₹374 against a first-order contribution of ₹1,650 × 50% − ₹374 = ₹825 − ₹374 = +₹451, acquisition is excellent — cheap, 4.4 ROAS, profitable on the first payment. Chasing it lower would be optimising the part that already works.

The number that should stop you cold is 7% repeat over 90 days. For SaaS, that's not a retention dip — it's a fire. Your whole model depends on customers staying and paying month after month; that's where the lifetime value lives. A 7% 90-day repeat means clinics sign up, pay once or twice, and churn out almost completely. You're acquiring beautifully into a product they don't stick with.

So the problem was never CAC, and making acquisition cheaper just fills a leaking tank more efficiently — you'd still lose them in 90 days. The leverage is entirely on retention: why do clinics leave? Onboarding that never gets them to first value, a missing workflow, no reason to log back in. Fix the reason they churn and that ₹451 first-order contribution turns into months of recurring margin. Don't spend a rupee optimising CAC until clinics stop walking out the back door.
